--- title: "Introduction to dagitty" --- Below is a guide to the **R package `dagitty`** (current CRAN version 0.3-4), keeping the same structure but adding depth: mathematical rationale, plain-English assumptions, multiple examples (basic + advanced), scaffolding steps, and common pitfalls. Citations point to the official reference manual, vignettes, and peer-reviewed overviews of `dagitty`. [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) # 1. Graph Construction & Manipulation ## 1.1 `dagitty()` — Parse DAGitty Syntax **What it does.** Builds a graph object from a short textual spec; supports DAGs and ancestral graphs (MAGs). Use the optional `layout=TRUE` to auto-generate node coordinates. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/dagitty?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Mathematical/causal rationale.** A DAG encodes a set of conditional independencies via **d-separation**. Edges `A -> B` represent direct causal effects (possibly with nonlinear/unknown functional form). In DAGitty syntax, bidirected edges `<->` stand for *latent* common causes (a shorthand for `A <- U -> B`). MAGs additionally allow undirected `--` edges for selection effects. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/dagitty?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Basic example (scaffold).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(dagitty) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ X -> Y; Z -> X }") # minimal confounding structure exposures(g) <- "X" outcomes(g) <- "Y" # mark roles for later tools g ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` dag { X [exposure] Y [outcome] Z X -> Y Z -> X } ``` ::: ::: This sets up a DAG where $Z$ is a cause of $X$ (a potential confounder for $X→Y$). [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Advanced example (MAG with latent + selection).**s ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g_mag <- dagitty("mag{ X <-> U <-> Y ; X -- S -- Y }") graphType(g_mag) # "mag" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "mag" ``` ::: ::: This MAG marks both latent confounding (`<->`) and selection (`--`). MAGs generalize DAGs for testable implications and equivalence. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/graphType?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ### Pitfalls & caveats - Prefer a strictly acyclic structure (`isAcyclic(g)`) to use standard DAG rules; MAGs are for advanced use. [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - Always set `exposures()` and `outcomes()` before computing adjustment sets or IVs. [oai_citation:6‡cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/refman/dagitty.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 1.2 `convert()` — Export to other Frameworks **What it does.** Converts a DAGitty graph into formats for **lavaan**, **bnlearn**, **tikz**, or **causaleffect** packages. Useful for moving from qualitative design to model specification/estimation. [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Example (to lavaan).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ X -> Y ; Z -> X ; Z -> Y }") model_string <- convert(g, to = "lavaan") cat(model_string) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Please set lavaan's fixed.x appopriately! Y~X X~Z Y~Z ``` ::: ::: Feed `model_string` to `lavaan::sem()` if you want to fit a linear SEM (note: causal identification ≠ statistical identifiability; verify assumptions). [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 1.3 `completeDAG()` **What it does.** Creates a fully connected DAG over given nodes; handy for stress tests and teaching. [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/man/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Example.** ``` r completeDAG(c("A", "B", "C")) ``` # 2. Graph Visualization & Layout ## 2.1 `graphLayout()` And `coordinates()` **What they do.** `graphLayout()` assigns positions (spring layout). `coordinates()` gets/sets positions; coordinates can be stored inside the DAGitty string or assigned afterward. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/graphLayout?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Scaffolded example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #| g <- dagitty("dag{ X->Y ; Z->X }") g <- graphLayout(g, "spring") # auto layout plot(g) # base plot method ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dagitty_files/figure-html/graph-layout-example-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coords <- coordinates(g) # retrieve coordinates(g) <- coords # could modify and set back ``` ::: For publication-grade plots in a tidyverse workflow, pair with **ggdag** (built on DAGitty). [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggdag/vignettes/intro-to-ggdag.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10869111/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Pitfall.** The spring layout is stochastic; call repeatedly or set seeds if you need stable figures. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/graphLayout?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 2.2 `plot.dagitty()` **What it does.** Quick base plotting for DAGs/MAGs; respects stored coordinates. Use **ggdag** for more control and theming. [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) # 3. Structural Queries & Relationships ## 3.1 Familial & Markov Relations **What they do.** `parents()`, `children()`, `ancestors()`, `descendants()`, `spouses()`, `markovBlanket()`. These map local neighborhoods and influence sets. The Markov blanket of node $V$ (its parents, children, and the parents of its children) renders $V$ independent of all other nodes given the blanket. [oai_citation:15‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/AncestralRelations?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Basic example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y ; Z->Y; U->Z->Y; Y-> O ->K }") plot(g) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dagitty_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat('Ancestors of Y:\n') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ancestors of Y: ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ancestors(g, "Y") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Y" "Z" "U" "X" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat('Descendants of Y:\n') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Descendants of Y: ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} descendants(g, "Y") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Y" "O" "K" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat('Children of Z:\n') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Children of Z: ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} parents(g, "Y") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "X" "Z" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat('Parents of Z:\n') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Parents of Z: ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} children(g, "Z") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "X" "Y" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat('Markov blanket of X:\n') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Markov blanket of X: ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} markovBlanket(g, "X") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Z" "Y" ``` ::: ::: **Advanced example (reasoning).** For feature selection in prediction (not causal): conditioning on a node’s Markov blanket is sufficient (though not always minimal) to predict that node. Don’t confuse predictive sufficiency with causal sufficiency. [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/man/AncestralRelations.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Common misconception.** “Ancestors/descendants exclude the node.” In DAGitty, `ancestors()` and `descendants()` include the node itself unless `proper=TRUE`. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/AncestralRelations?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 3.2 `paths()` **What it does.** Lists paths between exposure(s) and outcome(s) and whether they’re open (d-connected) or closed (d-separated) under a conditioning set $Z$. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/paths?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Plain-English d-separation rule.** A path is **blocked** if (i) it contains a **non-collider** that is conditioned on, or (ii) it contains a **collider** (or a descendant of a collider) that is **not** conditioned on. Otherwise, it’s **open**. Identifying open backdoor paths is the core of confounding control. (DAGitty manual gives a succinct overview.) [DAGitty](https://www.dagitty.net/manual-3.x.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Basic example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y ; Z->Y }") paths(g, from = "X", to = "Y") # backdoor X <- Z -> Y is open ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $paths [1] "X -> Y" "X <- Z -> Y" $open [1] TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} paths(g, from = "X", to = "Y", Z = list("Z")) # conditioning on Z closes it ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $paths [1] "X -> Y" "X <- Z -> Y" $open [1] TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: **Advanced example (collider bias).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ X->Y ; X->M<-U->Y }") # M is collider on X-M-U-Y paths(g, "X", "Y") # backdoor X <- U -> Y is closed by M ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $paths [1] "X -> M <- U -> Y" "X -> Y" $open [1] FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} paths(g, "X", "Y", Z = list("M")) # conditioning on M OPENS it (collider bias) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $paths [1] "X -> M <- U -> Y" "X -> Y" $open [1] TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: Use `paths()` to *explain* why an adjustment set works (or doesn’t). [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/paths?utm_source=chatgpt.com) # 4. Causal Analysis: Adjustment, Separation, Instruments ## 4.1 `adjustmentSets()` — Valid Covariates for Identification **What it does.** Enumerates **valid** sets $Z$ that block all backdoor paths from $X$ to $Y$ (for the **total** effect), optionally returning minimal sets or a “canonical” superset. **Assumption:** the graph is correct (edges capture the true causal relations and measured/latent status). [search.r-project.org](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/dagitty/html/adjustmentSets.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Backdoor identification formula (plain English).** If $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion, then the interventional mean is identifiable as $$ \mathbb{E}[Y\!\mid\!\mathrm{do}(X=x)] \;=\; \sum_{z} \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=x, Z=z]\, P(Z=z), $$ or with integrals for continuous $Z$. In practice: regress $Y$ on $X$ and $Z$ (correct functional form) or use standardization/IPW consistent with the DAG. The *validity* of $Z$ is a **graphical** condition. [DAGitty](https://www.dagitty.net/manual-3.x.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Scaffolded examples.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y ; Z->Y }") exposures(g) <- "X" outcomes(g) <- "Y" adjustmentSets(g, type = "minimal") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { Z } ``` ::: ::: **Advanced (M-bias).** Adjusting for a *pre-treatment* variable can hurt when it is a collider or on a path that opens bias. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ X->Y ; X <-> M <-> Y }") # M encodes latent U via <-> shorthands adjustmentSets(g, "X", "Y") # returns empty set; don't adjust for M ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {} ``` ::: ::: The reference manual shows simulation confirming bias inflation when wrongly adjusting. [oai_citation:23‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/adjustmentSets?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Nuances & pitfalls.** - For **direct effects**, specify `effect="direct"`; valid sets then must also block **mediator** paths. Interpret carefully. [oai_citation:24‡search.r-project.org](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/dagitty/html/adjustmentSets.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - Don’t auto-adjust for everything observed; that can open colliders or induce M-bias. Use the DAG. [oai_citation:25‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/adjustmentSets?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 4.2 `instrumentalVariables()` — Detect Candidate IVs **What it does.** Finds variables that satisfy graphical IV criteria relative to $(X,Y)$. **Assumptions (linear SEM context):** (i) relevance (IV→X), (ii) exclusion (no direct path IV→Y except via X), and (iii) independence from unmeasured causes of $Y$. Graphical discovery is heuristic and typically assumes linearity for certain algorithms. [oai_citation:26‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/instrumentalVariables?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Basic example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y ; Z<->U->Y }") # if Z has no path to Y except via X, it's an IV exposures(g) <- "X" outcomes(g) <- "Y" instrumentalVariables(g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Z | U ``` ::: ::: **Advanced note.** A variable can be a *conditional* IV given covariates; you must verify no open backdoor from IV to $Y$ after conditioning. Practical estimation typically uses 2SLS; discovery here is *graph-based* only. [oai_citation:27‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/instrumentalVariables?utm_source=chatgpt.com) # 5. Testing & Model Implications ## 5.1 `impliedConditionalIndependencies()` — D-separation Claims **What it does.** Lists CIs (e.g., $A \perp B \mid C$) that *must* hold for any distribution compatible with the graph. These implications can be confronted with data. [oai_citation:28‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/impliedConditionalIndependencies?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Use a graph with a non-trivial implied CI: Z ⟂⟂ Y | X g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y }") impliedConditionalIndependencies(g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Y _||_ Z | X ``` ::: ::: ## 5.2 `localTests()` + `plotLocalTestResults()` **What they do.** Derive testable implications from the graph and test them with data (partial correlations for continuous, appropriate associations for categorical); visualize effect sizes and CIs. **Caveat:** Passing tests does not *prove* the graph; failing tests falsifies it. [search.r-project.org](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/dagitty/html/localTests.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [currentprotocols.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://currentprotocols.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/cpz1.45?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Scaffolded example (continuous).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) # Use a DAG with at least one implied CI (Z ⟂⟂ Y | X) g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y }") exposures(g) <- "X" outcomes(g) <- "Y" d <- simulateSEM(g, N = 1000) # quick toy data res <- localTests(g, data = d) # tests graph-implied CIs (e.g., Z ⟂⟂ Y | X) head(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Guard against graphs with no testable implications if (is.data.frame(res) && ncol(res) > 0 && nrow(res) > 0) { plotLocalTestResults(res) } else { message("No testable implications for this graph; nothing to plot.") } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dagitty_files/figure-html/local-tests-example-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Advanced (categorical).** The protocol paper provides a workflow for DAG testing with categorical data (uses appropriate tests under the hood). [oai_citation:31‡currentprotocols.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://currentprotocols.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/cpz1.45?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Pitfalls.** - **Measurement error** can break expected CIs; consider latent measurement structure. [oai_citation:32‡cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - **Overconditioning** can induce dependencies (e.g., conditioning on a collider). Tests may “fail” because the analysis conditioned on the wrong set. ## 5.3 `vanishingTetrads()` **What it does.** Lists **tetrad constraints** of linear SEMs implied by the graph: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(i,j)\operatorname{Cov}(k,l) - \operatorname{Cov}(i,k)\operatorname{Cov}(j,l) \;=\; 0, $$ useful for model equivalence checks. These hold in particular causal structures (no correlated residuals) and can be empirically checked. [oai_citation:33‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/vanishingTetrads?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ A->C ; B->C ; A->D ; B->D }") # classic tetrad pattern vanishingTetrads(g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` list() ``` ::: ::: # 6. Simulation Utilities ## 6.1 `simulateSEM()` **What it does.** Treats the DAG as a *linear* SEM, draws random path coefficients (or use annotations), and simulates data; intended for validation/pedagogy rather than production simulations. [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/simulateSEM?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [search.r-project.org](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/dagitty/html/simulateSEM.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Basic example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ Z->X->Y ; Z->Y }") d <- simulateSEM(g, N = 1000) ``` ::: **Advanced (annotated coefficients).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- dagitty("dag{ Z -> X [beta=0.7]; X -> Y [beta=0.5]; Z -> Y [beta=0.1] }") d <- simulateSEM(g, N = 2000) ``` ::: **Tip.** For tidyverse workflows, `ggdag::simulate_data()` wraps `simulateSEM()` and returns tidied outputs. [r-causal.github.io](https://r-causal.github.io/ggdag/reference/simulate_data.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/ggdag/man/simulate_data.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 6.2 `simulateLogistic()` **What it does.** Simulates binary outcomes under logistic structural assumptions for quick experiments. (As with `simulateSEM()`, this is intentionally simple.) [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # 7. Graph Transformations & Checks ## 7.1 `canonicalize()` And `toMAG()` **What they do.** `canonicalize()` expands ancestral graphs into DAGs by replacing bidirected and undirected edges with explicit latent/selection nodes; `toMAG()` computes an observationally equivalent MAG, respecting marginalization over latents. These tools clarify where bias can arise (latent confounding vs. selection). [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/refman/dagitty.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [oai_citation:40‡Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) **Example.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Build a DAG with an unobserved common cause L of X and Y. g_dag <- dagitty("dag{ X <- L -> Y ; Z -> Y ; X -> Y; L [latent] }") plot(g_dag) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![DAG with a latent common causa L](dagitty_files/figure-html/fig-canonicalize-example-1.png){#fig-canonicalize-example width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Convert DAG -> MAG by marginalizing L; result is a MAG with X <-> Y g_mag <- toMAG(g_dag) graphType(g_mag) # "mag" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "mag" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Try to canonicalize; some dagitty versions don't support canonicalize() for MAG g_can <- tryCatch( canonicalize(g_mag), error = function(e) { message( "canonicalize() not supported for MAG in this dagitty version: ", e$message ) return(g_mag) } ) g_can ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $g dag { X Y Z X -> Y Z -> Y } $L list() $S list() ``` ::: ::: ## 7.2 `isAcyclic()`, `isAdjustmentSet()` **What they do.** Sanity checks—verify acyclicity and whether a proposed $Z$ truly satisfies the criterion (useful when you want to force a specific adjustment the algorithm didn’t return). [Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## 7.3 `backDoorGraph()` **What it does.** Produces the graph used by the backdoor algorithm (removes arrows out of $X$, etc.)—useful for teaching/diagnostics. [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # 8. Utility Functions & Examples - **`getExample()`** loads built-in classic DAGs (e.g., “Shrier”, “M-bias”) for demonstrations. [oai_citation:43‡Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/man/getExample.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)\ - **`downloadGraph()`** imports a DAG from **dagitty.net** by URL—handy when you sketch online, then continue in R. [oai_citation:44‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/downloadGraph?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [oai_citation:45‡DAGitty](https://www.dagitty.net/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)\ - **`edges()`** extracts edge lists (good for audits or exporting). [oai_citation:46‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/edges?utm_source=chatgpt.com)\ - **`graphType()`**, **`names.dagitty()`**, **`latents()`** inspect graph metadata and variable status (observed vs latent). [oai_citation:47‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/graphType?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [oai_citation:48‡Rdrr.io](https://rdrr.io/cran/dagitty/api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)\ - **Tidy/plot ecosystem.** `ggdag` provides high-level plotting, path visualization, and wrappers for many DAGitty computations (keeps DAGitty as the analytic engine). [oai_citation:49‡cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggdag/vignettes/intro-to-ggdag.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [oai_citation:50‡r-causal.r-universe.dev](https://r-causal.r-universe.dev/ggdag/doc/manual.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Summary Table (what to Reach for) | Purpose | Functions | Key ideas & cautions | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | Graph creation | `dagitty()`, `convert()`, `completeDAG()` | Encode causal knowledge first; set `exposures()`, `outcomes()` to prime later tools. [oai_citation:51‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/dagitty?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [oai_citation:52‡cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dagitty/dagitty.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) | | Plot/layout | `graphLayout()`, `coordinates()`, `plot()` | Layout is stochastic; store coordinates for reproducibility; consider `ggdag` for publication quality. [oai_citation:53‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/graphLayout?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [oai_citation:54‡cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggdag/vignettes/intro-to-ggdag.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) | | Local structure | `parents()`, `children()`, `ancestors()`, `descendants()`, `markovBlanket()` | Markov blanket is predictive, not necessarily causal; `ancestors()`/`descendants()` include node unless `proper=TRUE`. [oai_citation:55‡RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dagitty/versions/0.3-4/topics/AncestralRelations?utm_source=chatgpt.com) | | Paths & bias | `paths()` | Diagnose which paths remain open under conditioning; avoid conditioning on colliders.
